You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

And interestingly, and you know this well, IBM's market cap today is about 110 billion. The market cap of Microsoft is 10 times, it's over a trillion dollars. In the early 1980s, this young kid Bill Gates, Harvard School dropout, wrote the operating system DOS and sold it to IBM. And computer hardware is for their emerging personal computer. root   ::= "{" ws "\"claims\":" ws "[" ws (item (ws "," ws item){0,24})? ws "]" "," ws "\"fake_news\":" ws bool ws "}"
item   ::= "{" ws "\"phrase\":" ws string "," ws "\"stance\":" ws stance "," ws "\"verdict\":" ws verdict "," ws "\"evidence\":" ws string ws "}"
verdict ::= "\"FAKE_NEWS\"" | "\"NOT_FAKE_NEWS\"" | "\"UNVERIFIABLE\""

bool   ::= "true" | "false"
int    ::= [0-9]+
string ::= "\"" char* "\""
char   ::= [^"\\] | "\\" ["\\/bfnrt]
ws     ::= [ \t\n]{0,16}

messages.content:
You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

TRANSCRIPT (published 2026-07-12):
"Now, new questions are emerging about what federal health officials knew during the COVID vaccine rollout and whether the public was given the full picture about possible safety concerns. A recent Senate review led by Senator Ron Johnson is reviewing scrutiny of the vaccine adverse event reporting system known as VARES and how reports of possible side effects were handled during the pandemic. Joining us now to discuss is Dr. Ryan Cole, head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance. Thank you so much for joining us this morning. You bet, Angela. Thank you. So for people who may not be aware, what exactly is the vaccine adverse event reporting system? What's their role? What did they do during the COVID vaccine rollout? Sure, VARES has existed for about 30 years. It's an early reporting system to find safety signals. So it's basically the canary and the coal mine. And so when adverse events do occur after the rollout of something new, we have something to report to, whether it's a doctor, a family, or an individual. Okay. So something happens. Would people report to this system? Yes, they can. Okay. So Senator Ron Johnson, his review has raised new questions about how, you know, possible safety signals were handled. What do you believe the public needs to know at this point and what may not have been told at that time? Yeah, the important thing is that system does show those signals and there was a cover-up by the officials at FDA of the data that were coming in. So people lost the opportunity to make a risk-benefit choice to have informed consent in terms of getting that shot or not because we were seeing severe signals of harm that were covered up by the officials at the FDA that knew as early as March of 21 of things like sudden cardiac death, of strokes, of pulmonary emboli, that's clots to the lungs, things of that sort, which are life-threatening in nature. And yet officials in the government decided that we, the people, didn't need to know that. Now one of the issues here involves myocarditis, particularly among younger people. What do we know about those reports? Yeah, that's the other concerning area is we knew that young people were at very low risk for COVID, yet these shots carried that risk of heart damage and that heart damage we found can carry on with scarring later on in these young individuals. And again, it's a canary in the coal mine. These young individuals should have been given the option to avoid something that had early safety warnings that were ignored. Now as more information continues to come to light on this, what should patients and families who still have questions about vaccines or even possible side effects, what should they be doing now? So really quick, number one document, number two, it's not too late to do a retrospective report to the VAERS system. History matters. Number three, you find a friendly physician that will treat vaccine injury. And number four, always protect your rights and make sure that you keep track of government making sure that they stick to the policy that they have. All right, to learn more about the Independent Medical Alliance, visit imahealth.org. And thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Ryan Cole, the head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance."

TIME CHECK: the TRANSCRIPT contains time-bound wording ("at this point") and was published on 2026-07-12. A statement such as "so far" or "not yet" is about what was known when it was said; your knowledge extends past that date, so judge them against what was established at that date, not what was learned later.

string ::= "\"" char* "\""
char   ::= [^"\\] | "\\" ["\\/bfnrt]
ws     ::= [ \t\n]{0,16}

messages.content:
You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

TRANSCRIPT (published 2026-07-12):
"Now, new questions are emerging about what federal health officials knew during the COVID vaccine rollout and whether the public was given the full picture about possible safety concerns. A recent Senate review led by Senator Ron Johnson is reviewing scrutiny of the vaccine adverse event reporting system known as VARES and how reports of possible side effects were handled during the pandemic. Joining us now to discuss is Dr. Ryan Cole, head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance. Thank you so much for joining us this morning. You bet, Angela. Thank you. So for people who may not be aware, what exactly is the vaccine adverse event reporting system? What's their role? What did they do during the COVID vaccine rollout? Sure, VARES has existed for about 30 years. It's an early reporting system to find safety signals. So it's basically the canary and the coal mine. And so when adverse events do occur after the rollout of something new, we have something to report to, whether it's a doctor, a family, or an individual. Okay. So something happens. Would people report to this system? Yes, they can. Okay. So Senator Ron Johnson, his review has raised new questions about how, you know, possible safety signals were handled. What do you believe the public needs to know at this point and what may not have been told at that time? Yeah, the important thing is that system does show those signals and there was a cover-up by the officials at FDA of the data that were coming in. So people lost the opportunity to make a risk-benefit choice to have informed consent in terms of getting that shot or not because we were seeing severe signals of harm that were covered up by the officials at the FDA that knew as early as March of 21 of things like sudden cardiac death, of strokes, of pulmonary emboli, that's clots to the lungs, things of that sort, which are life-threatening in nature. And yet officials in the government decided that we, the people, didn't need to know that. Now one of the issues here involves myocarditis, particularly among younger people. What do we know about those reports? Yeah, that's the other concerning area is we knew that young people were at very low risk for COVID, yet these shots carried that risk of heart damage and that heart damage we found can carry on with scarring later on in these young individuals. And again, it's a canary in the coal mine. These young individuals should have been given the option to avoid something that had early safety warnings that were ignored. Now as more information continues to come to light on this, what should patients and families who still have questions about vaccines or even possible side effects, what should they be doing now? So really quick, number one document, number two, it's not too late to do a retrospective report to the VAERS system. History matters. Number three, you find a friendly physician that will treat vaccine injury. And number four, always protect your rights and make sure that you keep track of government making sure that they stick to the policy that they have. All right, to learn more about the Independent Medical Alliance, visit imahealth.org. And thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Ryan Cole, the head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance."

TIME CHECK: the TRANSCRIPT contains time-bound wording ("at this point") and was published on 2026-07-12. A statement such as "so far" or "not yet" is about what was known when it was said; your knowledge extends past that date, so judge them against what was established at that date, not what was learned later.

messages.content:
You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

TRANSCRIPT (published 2026-07-12):
"Now, new questions are emerging about what federal health officials knew during the COVID vaccine rollout and whether the public was given the full picture about possible safety concerns. A recent Senate review led by Senator Ron Johnson is reviewing scrutiny of the vaccine adverse event reporting system known as VARES and how reports of possible side effects were handled during the pandemic. Joining us now to discuss is Dr. Ryan Cole, head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance. Thank you so much for joining us this morning. You bet, Angela. Thank you. So for people who may not be aware, what exactly is the vaccine adverse event reporting system? What's their role? What did they do during the COVID vaccine rollout? Sure, VARES has existed for about 30 years. It's an early reporting system to find safety signals. So it's basically the canary and the coal mine. And so when adverse events do occur after the rollout of something new, we have something to report to, whether it's a doctor, a family, or an individual. Okay. So something happens. Would people report to this system? Yes, they can. Okay. So Senator Ron Johnson, his review has raised new questions about how, you know, possible safety signals were handled. What do you believe the public needs to know at this point and what may not have been told at that time? Yeah, the important thing is that system does show those signals and there was a cover-up by the officials at FDA of the data that were coming in. So people lost the opportunity to make a risk-benefit choice to have informed consent in terms of getting that shot or not because we were seeing severe signals of harm that were covered up by the officials at the FDA that knew as early as March of 21 of things like sudden cardiac death, of strokes, of pulmonary emboli, that's clots to the lungs, things of that sort, which are life-threatening in nature. And yet officials in the government decided that we, the people, didn't need to know that. Now one of the issues here involves myocarditis, particularly among younger people. What do we know about those reports? Yeah, that's the other concerning area is we knew that young people were at very low risk for COVID, yet these shots carried that risk of heart damage and that heart damage we found can carry on with scarring later on in these young individuals. And again, it's a canary in the coal mine. These young individuals should have been given the option to avoid something that had early safety warnings that were ignored. Now as more information continues to come to light on this, what should patients and families who still have questions about vaccines or even possible side effects, what should they be doing now? So really quick, number one document, number two, it's not too late to do a retrospective report to the VAERS system. History matters. Number three, you find a friendly physician that will treat vaccine injury. And number four, always protect your rights and make sure that you keep track of government making sure that they stick to the policy that they have. All right, to learn more about the Independent Medical Alliance, visit imahealth.org. And thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Ryan Cole, the head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance."

TIME CHECK: the TRANSCRIPT contains time-bound wording ("at this point") and was published on 2026-07-12. A statement such as "so far" or "not yet" is about what was known when it was said; your knowledge extends past that date, so judge them against what was established at that date, not what was learned later.

You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

TRANSCRIPT (published 2025-05-05):
"A groundbreaking new study sounding alarms about the safety of COVID mRNA vaccines directly challenging claims from public health officials and raising urgent questions about transparency and trust. So using hard data from disease trends from patient outcomes and immune system analysis, multiple research reports show that heart inflammation risks tied to the vaccines maybe far greater and maybe even more dangerous than previously reported, particularly among young men joining us now to discuss this as Independent Medical Alliance Senior Fellow of Pediatric Cardiology, Dr. Kirk Milhome. Good morning to you, doctor. Welcome to the national news desk. Great to have you. Good morning. Thanks for having me on. This new study about the safety of COVID mRNA vaccines was published in the International Journal of Cardiovascular Research and Innovation, as I understand it. Tell us about the scope of this research and really your top findings from it. So it's a compilation of studies that really have been out there since 2021. We saw a signal in, um, the vaccine product causing problems, especially in the young adults, especially young males that was causing heart inflammation. And so what we have done is compiled all those different peer review journals, articles and data and put them in one place easily accessible with 42 pages and 341 references of our concerns This is a real issue and these vaccines do little good for healthy children and young adults, right? Were you able to distinguish the cause of myocarditis, the differential between a COVID infection versus it being just an adverse reaction to the COVID vaccine? Yes, it's very, it's very clear from the number of reasons that we've been able to evaluate and primarily there was a great study out of the Nordic countries that studied 23 million children and young adults and they found that the people who had the least amount of myocarditis were the unvaccinated and as you increased the number of vaccine doses or you used Moderna versus Pfizer, your risk just kept stepping up in terms of your risk for myocarditis. Once again, in a disease state that is really very mild for healthy children and young adults. You know, initially this topic was so rare when we first heard about this, myocarditis and the links, you know, to the vaccine but what does the data reveal now? So there was a study out of Lancet that showed and looked at all these children who had been harmed by the vaccine and received and had myocarditis secondary to the vaccine and they looked at them 90 days out and a lot of things remain normal except their cardiac MRI which showed and continued inflammation and possible scarring of the heart itself 90 days out. Further studies, a new study released by Yale said that they're still having free-floating spike protein which is what that vaccine asks the body to make which is a cardiotoxin still floating around in the body for over 700 days. It was supposed to just be put in and your body had a new response and then it went away but it is hanging around in some pieces. So it's not transitory it's not resolving over time. I mean there's like long-term impacts we're seeing right now. Yeah, for certain people it is devastating and long-term processes that they had very little risk for. Wow. So for more information you can visit imahealth.org and doctor we appreciate you joining us this morning to talk about this very important topic. Thank you for having me on."

item   ::= "{" ws "\"phrase\":" ws string "," ws "\"stance\":" ws stance "," ws "\"verdict\":" ws verdict "," ws "\"evidence\":" ws string ws "}"
verdict ::= "\"FAKE_NEWS\"" | "\"NOT_FAKE_NEWS\"" | "\"UNVERIFIABLE\""

stance ::= "\"asserting\"" | "\"denying\"" | "\"neutral\""
bool   ::= "true" | "false"
int    ::= [0-9]+
string ::= "\"" char* "\""
char   ::= [^"\\] | "\\" ["\\/bfnrt]
ws     ::= [ \t\n]{0,16}

But according to a paper appearing in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, not all vaccines are created equal. We're talking about this paper, which compares myocarditis rates between the Pfizer and Moderna vaccines. And the differences are pretty stark. This is a huge study of more than 3 million individuals who received at least two doses of mRNA vaccine in British Columbia in 2021. Just over 70% received the Pfizer vaccine. Researchers linked those vaccine records to emergency room and hospitalization visits for myocarditis and pericarditis as defined by ICD-10 codes within 21 days of vaccination. On the side here, yes, ICD-10 codes are imperfect, but it seems like they were pretty specific in this study of the 59 cases of myocarditis identified, 57 had a troponin measured, and 51 of those were elevated. Of course, it's possible that there are more cases of myocarditis that were never captured, either because the individual did not seek care or the diagnosis was missed. First of all, let's get oriented to the Y axis. The background rate of myocarditis, pre-pandemic, pre-vaccine, is about two per million. messages.content:
You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

request.grammar:
root   ::= "{" ws "\"claims\":" ws "[" ws (item (ws "," ws item){0,24})? ws "]" "," ws "\"fake_news\":" ws bool ws "}"
item   ::= "{" ws "\"phrase\":" ws string "," ws "\"stance\":" ws stance "," ws "\"verdict\":" ws verdict "," ws "\"evidence\":" ws string ws "}"
verdict ::= "\"FAKE_NEWS\"" | "\"NOT_FAKE_NEWS\"" | "\"UNVERIFIABLE\""

# Bounded on purpose (2026-11-11): unbounded ws let gemma-4-12b pad a reply with
# newlines until the token cap, and an unbounded array let it list 86 claims
# against an instruction of at most MAX_CLAIMS. {0,24} = MAX_CLAIMS - 1 more items.
stance ::= "\"asserting\"" | "\"denying\"" | "\"neutral\""
bool   ::= "true" | "false"
int    ::= [0-9]+
string ::= "\"" char* "\""
char   ::= [^"\\] | "\\" ["\\/bfnrt]
ws     ::= [ \t\n]{0,16}

You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

TRANSCRIPT (published 2026-07-12):
"Now, new questions are emerging about what federal health officials knew during the COVID vaccine rollout and whether the public was given the full picture about possible safety concerns. A recent Senate review led by Senator Ron Johnson is reviewing scrutiny of the vaccine adverse event reporting system known as VARES and how reports of possible side effects were handled during the pandemic. Joining us now to discuss is Dr. Ryan Cole, head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance. Thank you so much for joining us this morning. You bet, Angela. Thank you. So for people who may not be aware, what exactly is the vaccine adverse event reporting system? What's their role? What did they do during the COVID vaccine rollout? Sure, VARES has existed for about 30 years. It's an early reporting system to find safety signals. So it's basically the canary and the coal mine. And so when adverse events do occur after the rollout of something new, we have something to report to, whether it's a doctor, a family, or an individual. Okay. So something happens. Would people report to this system? Yes, they can. Okay. So Senator Ron Johnson, his review has raised new questions about how, you know, possible safety signals were handled. What do you believe the public needs to know at this point and what may not have been told at that time? Yeah, the important thing is that system does show those signals and there was a cover-up by the officials at FDA of the data that were coming in. So people lost the opportunity to make a risk-benefit choice to have informed consent in terms of getting that shot or not because we were seeing severe signals of harm that were covered up by the officials at the FDA that knew as early as March of 21 of things like sudden cardiac death, of strokes, of pulmonary emboli, that's clots to the lungs, things of that sort, which are life-threatening in nature. And yet officials in the government decided that we, the people, didn't need to know that. Now one of the issues here involves myocarditis, particularly among younger people. What do we know about those reports? Yeah, that's the other concerning area is we knew that young people were at very low risk for COVID, yet these shots carried that risk of heart damage and that heart damage we found can carry on with scarring later on in these young individuals. And again, it's a canary in the coal mine. These young individuals should have been given the option to avoid something that had early safety warnings that were ignored. Now as more information continues to come to light on this, what should patients and families who still have questions about vaccines or even possible side effects, what should they be doing now? So really quick, number one document, number two, it's not too late to do a retrospective report to the VAERS system. History matters. Number three, you find a friendly physician that will treat vaccine injury. And number four, always protect your rights and make sure that you keep track of government making sure that they stick to the policy that they have. All right, to learn more about the Independent Medical Alliance, visit imahealth.org. And thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Ryan Cole, the head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance."

TIME CHECK: the TRANSCRIPT contains time-bound wording ("at this point") and was published on 2026-07-12. A statement such as "so far" or "not yet" is about what was known when it was said; your knowledge extends past that date, so judge them against what was established at that date, not what was learned later.

messages.content:
You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

TRANSCRIPT (published 2026-07-12):
"Now, new questions are emerging about what federal health officials knew during the COVID vaccine rollout and whether the public was given the full picture about possible safety concerns. A recent Senate review led by Senator Ron Johnson is reviewing scrutiny of the vaccine adverse event reporting system known as VARES and how reports of possible side effects were handled during the pandemic. Joining us now to discuss is Dr. Ryan Cole, head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance. Thank you so much for joining us this morning. You bet, Angela. Thank you. So for people who may not be aware, what exactly is the vaccine adverse event reporting system? What's their role? What did they do during the COVID vaccine rollout? Sure, VARES has existed for about 30 years. It's an early reporting system to find safety signals. So it's basically the canary and the coal mine. And so when adverse events do occur after the rollout of something new, we have something to report to, whether it's a doctor, a family, or an individual. Okay. So something happens. Would people report to this system? Yes, they can. Okay. So Senator Ron Johnson, his review has raised new questions about how, you know, possible safety signals were handled. What do you believe the public needs to know at this point and what may not have been told at that time? Yeah, the important thing is that system does show those signals and there was a cover-up by the officials at FDA of the data that were coming in. So people lost the opportunity to make a risk-benefit choice to have informed consent in terms of getting that shot or not because we were seeing severe signals of harm that were covered up by the officials at the FDA that knew as early as March of 21 of things like sudden cardiac death, of strokes, of pulmonary emboli, that's clots to the lungs, things of that sort, which are life-threatening in nature. And yet officials in the government decided that we, the people, didn't need to know that. Now one of the issues here involves myocarditis, particularly among younger people. What do we know about those reports? Yeah, that's the other concerning area is we knew that young people were at very low risk for COVID, yet these shots carried that risk of heart damage and that heart damage we found can carry on with scarring later on in these young individuals. And again, it's a canary in the coal mine. These young individuals should have been given the option to avoid something that had early safety warnings that were ignored. Now as more information continues to come to light on this, what should patients and families who still have questions about vaccines or even possible side effects, what should they be doing now? So really quick, number one document, number two, it's not too late to do a retrospective report to the VAERS system. History matters. Number three, you find a friendly physician that will treat vaccine injury. And number four, always protect your rights and make sure that you keep track of government making sure that they stick to the policy that they have. All right, to learn more about the Independent Medical Alliance, visit imahealth.org. And thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Ryan Cole, the head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance."

TIME CHECK: the TRANSCRIPT contains time-bound wording ("at this point") and was published on 2026-07-12. A statement such as "so far" or "not yet" is about what was known when it was said; your knowledge extends past that date, so judge them against what was established at that date, not what was learned later.

messages.content:
You are a fact-checking classifier. You are given the full TRANSCRIPT of a video. No evidence is provided: judge it from your own knowledge of the scientific and public-health consensus.

First find the factual claims in the TRANSCRIPT: statements about the world that could be checked, including ones the speaker denies, questions or only reports. Copy each as a short phrase of at most 30 words, verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT. List at most 25, most important first; skip greetings, advertising and small talk.

Then decide, for each claim, whether the speaker is asserting something that consensus contradicts, and finally whether the video contains fake news.

Verdicts for each claim:
- "FAKE_NEWS": the speaker asserts, implies, or presents as fact something the scientific and public-health consensus contradicts. This includes stating that a vaccine contains an ingredient it does not contain, or that it has an effect it does not have. It counts even if the speaker is vague, hedging, or embedding the claim in a longer story.
- "NOT_FAKE_NEWS": the speaker agrees with the consensus, or is quoting, reporting, questioning or debunking the false claim rather than asserting it.
- "UNVERIFIABLE": you cannot determine from your own knowledge whether what the speaker says is true or false, or it makes no checkable factual claim. Use this rather than guessing.

Key distinction: a speaker who DENIES a myth ("vaccines do not cause infertility") is NOT_FAKE_NEWS. A speaker who ASSERTS it is FAKE_NEWS.

Before deciding, determine the speaker's STANCE toward the false idea. Look for negations and denials: "isn't", "aren't", "not possible", "no reason to suspect", "there's no evidence", "that's a myth", "doesn't". If the speaker is saying the false thing is NOT true, the verdict is NOT_FAKE_NEWS even though the topic matches. Topic overlap alone is never enough to flag.

Reply with a JSON object using EXACTLY these two keys, in this order:
  "claims"    - a list with one object per claim, each with EXACTLY these keys in this order:
      "phrase"   - the claim, copied verbatim from the TRANSCRIPT
      "stance"   - "asserting" if the speaker presents the false idea as true, "denying" if they say it is false, "neutral" if merely describing or unclear
      "verdict"  - one of "FAKE_NEWS", "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "UNVERIFIABLE". Use FAKE_NEWS only when stance is "asserting".
      "evidence" - for FAKE_NEWS, one sentence on what the consensus says that contradicts the claim; otherwise an empty string
  "fake_news" - true if at least one claim is FAKE_NEWS, otherwise false

Example:
{"claims": [{"phrase": "the vaccine makes you magnetic", "stance": "asserting", "verdict": "FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": "COVID-19 vaccines contain no metals and cannot make a person magnetic."}, {"phrase": "vaccines do not cause infertility", "stance": "denying", "verdict": "NOT_FAKE_NEWS", "evidence": ""}], "fake_news": true}

JSON only.

TRANSCRIPT (published 2026-07-12):
"Now, new questions are emerging about what federal health officials knew during the COVID vaccine rollout and whether the public was given the full picture about possible safety concerns. A recent Senate review led by Senator Ron Johnson is reviewing scrutiny of the vaccine adverse event reporting system known as VARES and how reports of possible side effects were handled during the pandemic. Joining us now to discuss is Dr. Ryan Cole, head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance. Thank you so much for joining us this morning. You bet, Angela. Thank you. So for people who may not be aware, what exactly is the vaccine adverse event reporting system? What's their role? What did they do during the COVID vaccine rollout? Sure, VARES has existed for about 30 years. It's an early reporting system to find safety signals. So it's basically the canary and the coal mine. And so when adverse events do occur after the rollout of something new, we have something to report to, whether it's a doctor, a family, or an individual. Okay. So something happens. Would people report to this system? Yes, they can. Okay. So Senator Ron Johnson, his review has raised new questions about how, you know, possible safety signals were handled. What do you believe the public needs to know at this point and what may not have been told at that time? Yeah, the important thing is that system does show those signals and there was a cover-up by the officials at FDA of the data that were coming in. So people lost the opportunity to make a risk-benefit choice to have informed consent in terms of getting that shot or not because we were seeing severe signals of harm that were covered up by the officials at the FDA that knew as early as March of 21 of things like sudden cardiac death, of strokes, of pulmonary emboli, that's clots to the lungs, things of that sort, which are life-threatening in nature. And yet officials in the government decided that we, the people, didn't need to know that. Now one of the issues here involves myocarditis, particularly among younger people. What do we know about those reports? Yeah, that's the other concerning area is we knew that young people were at very low risk for COVID, yet these shots carried that risk of heart damage and that heart damage we found can carry on with scarring later on in these young individuals. And again, it's a canary in the coal mine. These young individuals should have been given the option to avoid something that had early safety warnings that were ignored. Now as more information continues to come to light on this, what should patients and families who still have questions about vaccines or even possible side effects, what should they be doing now? So really quick, number one document, number two, it's not too late to do a retrospective report to the VAERS system. History matters. Number three, you find a friendly physician that will treat vaccine injury. And number four, always protect your rights and make sure that you keep track of government making sure that they stick to the policy that they have. All right, to learn more about the Independent Medical Alliance, visit imahealth.org. And thank you so much for joining us, Dr. Ryan Cole, the head of the Medical and Scientific Affairs for the Independent Medical Alliance."

TIME CHECK: the TRANSCRIPT contains time-bound wording ("at this point") and was published on 2026-07-12. A statement such as "so far" or "not yet" is about what was known when it was said; your knowledge extends past that date, so judge them against what was established at that date, not what was learned later.

"Welcome to Impact Factor, your weekly dose of commentary on a new medical study. I'm Dr. F. Perry Wilson of the Yale School of Medicine. Let me start with a non-controversial statement. A small number of individuals who receive an mRNA vaccine will develop myocarditis. Myocarditis is a side effect of these vaccines, albeit a rare one. It's a side effect that has taken on an importance in the public consciousness that far outpaces its actual rate. For many people it serves as confirmation that their worst fears about the vaccines, that they were rushed through development without proper oversight, that they're part of a plot to depopulate the planet, that they contain tracking devices, are true. And we could try to explain how rare outcomes are rare or how the risk of myocarditis from COVID is likely higher than the risk of myocarditis from vaccines or how myocarditis is not the only outcome we need to worry about when it comes to COVID infection. But in the end, the fact that some people will experience myocarditis after vaccination gives an off-ramp to the vaccine hesitant, hindering public health efforts. But according to a paper appearing in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, not all vaccines are created equal. We're talking about this paper, which compares myocarditis rates between the Pfizer and Moderna vaccines. And the differences are pretty stark. This is a huge study of more than 3 million individuals who received at least two doses of mRNA vaccine in British Columbia in 2021. Just over 70% received the Pfizer vaccine. Researchers linked those vaccine records to emergency room and hospitalization visits for myocarditis and pericarditis as defined by ICD-10 codes within 21 days of vaccination. On the side here, yes, ICD-10 codes are imperfect, but it seems like they were pretty specific in this study of the 59 cases of myocarditis identified, 57 had a troponin measured, and 51 of those were elevated. Of course, it's possible that there are more cases of myocarditis that were never captured, either because the individual did not seek care or the diagnosis was missed. From here, the study is simple. The numerator is the number of cases of myocarditis, the denominator is the number of people vaccinated. And here's what you get. Lots to take home from this graph. First of all, let's get oriented to the Y axis. The background rate of myocarditis, pre-pandemic, pre-vaccine, is about two per million. So clearly the signal you see here is not just random background noise. As in prior studies, you can see the risk is highest among men and particularly younger men. But critically, you can see that the rate of myocarditis in those at risk groups is dramatically higher with the Moderna vaccine compared to Pfizer. That point is driven home in this time to event graph. You can see that myocarditis cases start to rise within a couple of days of vaccination with Moderna plateauing after a week or so. Pfizer, while clearly above baseline, has a substantially lower rate. If we focus in on those young men, you can see how the rates in this study compared to those measured by the CDC and for good measure, the rates seen in young college athletes recovering from a COVID infection. Again, it does seem that the risk from COVID far outpaces the risk from vaccination, but that risk outpaces the background rate of myocarditis. What's a young man to do? To be honest, it's complicated. And this study does not answer all the questions that we may have about this situation. There was no real control group. It didn't measure the rate of myocarditis among people who don't get the vaccine, though certainly the pre-COVID rate is quite a bit lower. There was no analysis of post-COVID myocarditis. I'm pulling numbers from other studies to make a comparison there. This study didn't look at other side effects from vaccination or the efficacy of vaccination against COVID infection, hospitalization or death. It didn't look at the myocarditis rate among those with a prior COVID infection or after a booster vaccine. Finally, though other studies have suggested that post-vaccine myocarditis is relatively mild, this one doesn't tell us how these patients fared. But it did tell us something really important, that there is a difference in the rate of this particular adverse event based on which mRNA vaccine is received. And for those who are going to get vaccinated, that may be a very useful piece of information. Particularly for young men, it seems like Pfizer is a better choice here. It may well be the lesser of three evils. For Medscape, I'm Perry Wilson."

"Now, switching gears in the race to vaccinate, we are continuing to get more real-world data about the vaccines and how they're working to discuss that. We're going to bring in our medical expert and friend, Dr. Arnold Baskie. He's the past chairman of the National Board of Directors of the American Cancer Society and also chair of the Global Cancer Control Advisory Council. Dr. B, good morning. Good morning, Stephanie. So this past week, we learned that an advisory panel for the CDC is investigating reports of heart inflammation in a small number of people who got the COVID-19 vaccine. Now, the CDC committee says that these cases have predominantly occurred in adolescents, young adults, predominantly male. If I'm a parent, my antennas immediately go up. So what can you tell us about this? So the breakthrough cases are important to remember that they can occur, that no vaccine is 100% effective in preventing illness. Here's what is important. However, between January 1st and April of 30th of this year, there were about 101 million people who were fully vaccinated and about 10,000 people tested positive. If you do the math, that means that about 0.01% of people tested positive after the vaccine, which also means that 99.99% of people did not test positive after the vaccine. So the vaccine is very, very effective. It's effective in all the age groups that we've been able to study, and that includes children of 12 and over. While 10,000 people out of 101 million is not exactly a trivial number, it is, from a total population point of view, very important to recognize that these vaccines are miracles, that they do work and that they do prevent infection. And that's really what we need to tell people, especially parents of children. So yeah, you just mentioned that. So you were talking about those breakthrough cases, obviously we've been hearing. You heard about the Yankees, right, that they were fully vaccinated, yet they still tested positive. Bill Maher, for example. But I want to go back to this other thing that we've been reading from the CDC, where they're investigating a small number of people who got the COVID-19 vaccine, and yet they found that predominantly adolescents, young adults, mostly male, had some kind of heart condition. Have you looked into that? What do we know about that? Well, currently there are a few rare scattered cases of what we call myocarditis, which is an inflammatory condition that affects the muscles of the heart. The best data that we have on this actually comes from Israel. And in Israel they were looking at the vaccines earlier than we were and have a really good handle on the side effects, the potential side effects for the vaccine. The bottom line is that in Israel, out of 5 million people who are vaccinated, there were about 62 cases of myocarditis that they felt was related to the vaccination. If it is going to occur, and it will occur rarely, it will be after the second dose and usually within four days of the shot. The rare condition seems to occur in men or teenagers between ages 16 to 30. So this is an unusual event. However, it gets better in the vast majority of people. It's a sign that the vaccine has created an inflammatory condition. And one of the things that can get affected is the heart muscle. But it's an extremely rare event and that's probably what the CDC is going to conclude when they look at all the data. Yeah, we needed to outline that just because obviously a lot of parents hear that and automatically get concerned. But like everything, you know, we're getting new information about the vaccine and its efficacy and apparently some of the side effects every week, but you're still saying either get the vaccine or the virus. That's right. And I can tell you that my grandchildren have all been vaccinated. They've done great. They've had no side effects. This is a very rare event. And by the way, with a little bit of moatrin, it tends, it gets better. So this is not a life-threatening type of problem, at least from the data that we have so far. Dr. B, as always, we love having you on. Happy Sunday. Same to you, Stephanie."
